title: Magnification and Unit Conversions
description: Calculate magnification, image size and actual size — and convert confidently between mm, μm and nm.

method_card.title: Magnification and Unit Conversions
method_card.content:
Magnification questions always involve three quantities — magnification, image size and actual size. You'll be given two and asked to find the third.

Approach:

  1. Identify which quantity you need to find
  2. Check the units — both sizes must be in the same unit before you divide
  3. Convert if needed: multiply by 1000 going smaller (mm → μm → nm), divide by 1000 going larger
  4. Substitute and calculate
  5. If asked for actual size, rearrange: actual size = image size ÷ magnification

Common pitfalls:

  • Forgetting to convert units before dividing — if image is in mm and real size is in μm, convert one first
  • Dividing the wrong way round — magnification = image ÷ actual, NOT actual ÷ image
  • Leaving magnification with a unit — magnification has no unit
  • Standard form errors — count your zeros carefully for very small cell sizes
steps: Identify what you need to find: magnification, image size, or actual size
Check units — convert both sizes to the same unit before calculating
Use ×1000 going smaller (mm→μm→nm) or ÷1000 going larger (nm→μm→mm)
Substitute into the magnification equation and calculate
State your answer with the correct unit (magnification has no unit)

exam_context.frequency: Very common — appears regularly and links to Required Practical 1 (microscopy)

worked_examples.question: A cell has an actual size of 50 μm. Under a microscope the image measures 25 mm. Calculate the magnification.
An image of a bacterium is 30 mm long under a magnification of ×10,000. Calculate the actual size of the bacterium in μm.
A mitochondrion has an actual length of 2 μm. A student draws it 60 mm long. Calculate the actual size in metres and give your answer in standard form.

steps.label: Step 1 — Convert actual size to metres
Step 2 — This is already the actual size
steps.content: The question asks for the actual size in metres — we just convert the given 2 μm.

bronze.display: A plant cell has an actual size of 100 μm. Under a microscope the image is 40 mm long. Calculate the magnification. (Convert the image to μm first.)

misconceptions.message: Convert the image to μm first: 40 mm = 40,000 μm. Then 40,000 ÷ 100 = ×400.
Magnification = image ÷ actual, not actual ÷ image. 40,000 ÷ 100 = 400.

bronze.display: Convert 0.5 mm to μm.

misconceptions.message: Going from mm to μm means going smaller, so multiply by 1000. 0.5 × 1000 = 500 μm.

bronze.display: A cheek cell is 60 μm across. An image of it is 12 mm across. What is the magnification?

misconceptions.message: Convert image to μm: 12 mm = 12,000 μm. Magnification = 12,000 ÷ 60 = ×200.
Magnification = image ÷ actual = 12,000 ÷ 60 = 200, not 60 ÷ 12,000.

bronze.display: Convert 7500 μm to mm.

misconceptions.message: Going from μm to mm means going larger, so divide by 1000. 7500 ÷ 1000 = 7.5 mm.

bronze.display: A microscope has a magnification of ×400. The image of a cell is 20 mm long. What is the actual size of the cell in μm?

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 20 mm = 20,000 μm. Then 20,000 ÷ 400 = 50 μm.
Convert the image to μm before dividing: 20 mm = 20,000 μm. 20,000 ÷ 400 = 50 μm.

bronze.display: Convert 3 μm to nm.

misconceptions.message: Going from μm to nm means going smaller, so multiply by 1000. 3 × 1000 = 3000 nm.

bronze.display: An onion cell has an actual width of 80 μm. A student draws it 24 mm wide. Calculate the magnification.

misconceptions.message: Convert: 24 mm = 24,000 μm. Magnification = 24,000 ÷ 80 = ×300.

bronze.display: Which of these is the correct unit conversion?

misconceptions.message: 1 mm = 1000 μm. Think: milli = 10⁻³, micro = 10⁻⁶, so there are 10³ = 1000 μm in 1 mm.

silver.display: A bacterium has an actual length of 2 μm. A photograph shows it as 15 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the photograph.

misconceptions.message: Convert: 15 mm = 15,000 μm. Magnification = 15,000 ÷ 2 = ×7500.
Magnification = image ÷ actual = 15,000 ÷ 2 = 7500. If you got 0.000133, you divided the wrong way.

silver.display: An image of a cell is 36 mm long. The magnification used was ×1200. Calculate the actual size of the cell in μm.

misconceptions.message: Actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 36 mm = 36,000 μm. Then 36,000 ÷ 1200 = 30 μm.
Convert image to μm first: 36 mm = 36,000 μm. Then 36,000 ÷ 1200 = 30 μm.

silver.display: A red blood cell has a diameter of 7 μm. A student wants to draw it with a magnification of ×2000. How long should the drawing be, in mm?

misconceptions.message: Image = magnification × actual = 2000 × 7 = 14,000 μm = 14 mm.
Image size = 2000 × 7 = 14,000 μm. Convert to mm: 14,000 ÷ 1000 = 14 mm.

silver.display: A micrograph shows a sperm cell head as 8 mm across at ×5000 magnification. Calculate the actual size of the sperm head in μm.

misconceptions.message: Actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 8 mm = 8000 μm. Then 8000 ÷ 5000 = 1.6 μm.

silver.display: An E. coli bacterium is 2 μm long. Express this length in metres, giving your answer in standard form.

misconceptions.message: 1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m. So 2 μm = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m. The exponent is −6, not −3 (that would be mm).

silver.display: A palisade cell is 0.035 mm long. Convert this to μm.

misconceptions.message: mm to μm: multiply by 1000. 0.035 × 1000 = 35 μm.
0.035 × 1000 = 35, not 3.5 or 350. Move the decimal point 3 places right.

gold.display: A ribosome has a diameter of 25 nm. Express this in metres, giving your answer in standard form.

misconceptions.message: 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m. So 25 nm = 25 × 10⁻⁹ m = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ m. Adjust to correct standard form.
nm to m: 25 nm = 25 × 10⁻⁹ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ m. Don't confuse nm (10⁻⁹) with μm (10⁻⁶).

gold.display: An electron micrograph shows a mitochondrion at ×40,000 magnification. The image is 80 mm long. Calculate the actual length in μm.

misconceptions.message: Actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 80 mm = 80,000 μm. Then 80,000 ÷ 40,000 = 2 μm.
You must convert mm to μm before dividing: 80 mm = 80,000 μm. 80,000 ÷ 40,000 = 2 μm.

gold.display: A white blood cell has an actual diameter of 12 μm. A red blood cell has an actual diameter of 7 μm. How many times wider is the white blood cell than the red blood cell? Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: Divide the larger by the smaller: 12 ÷ 7 = 1.714… ≈ 1.7 times wider.
The question asks how many times wider, so divide (12 ÷ 7 ≈ 1.7), don't subtract (12 − 7 = 5).

gold.display: A student measures an image of a cell as 45 mm. The actual cell is 0.015 mm. Calculate the magnification, then determine if this cell is likely to be a bacterium (1–5 μm), an animal cell (10–30 μm), or a plant cell (10–100 μm).

misconceptions.message: Magnification = 45 ÷ 0.015 = 3000. Actual size = 0.015 mm = 15 μm. This fits 10–30 μm = animal cell.
0.015 mm = 15 μm (multiply by 1000). 15 μm fits the range of an animal cell (10–30 μm).

gold.display: A virus is 300 nm in diameter. An electron microscope produces an image 18 mm across. Calculate the magnification.

misconceptions.message: Convert image: 18 mm = 18,000 μm = 18,000,000 nm. Magnification = 18,000,000 ÷ 300 = ×60,000.

gold.display: A student measures the image of a bacterial cell as 14 mm under ×4000 magnification. Another student measures the image of a plant cell as 48 mm under ×800 magnification. Which cell has the larger actual size, and by how many μm?

misconceptions.message: Bacterium: 14 mm = 14,000 μm, actual = 14,000 ÷ 4000 = 3.5 μm. Plant: 48 mm = 48,000 μm, actual = 48,000 ÷ 800 = 60 μm. Difference = 60 − 3.5 = 56.5 μm.
Don't compare image sizes — compare actual sizes. A larger image doesn't mean a larger cell if the magnification is higher.

title: Punnett Squares and Genetic Probability
description: Complete Punnett square crosses, calculate offspring ratios and percentages, and determine genotypes from results.

method_card.title: Punnett Squares and Genetic Probability
method_card.content:
Punnett squares show all the possible combinations of alleles that offspring can inherit from two parents.

Key terminology:

  • Dominant allele — shown with a capital letter (e.g. B) — always expressed if present
  • Recessive allele — shown with a lowercase letter (e.g. b) — only expressed when two copies are present (bb)
  • Homozygous — two identical alleles (BB or bb)
  • Heterozygous — two different alleles (Bb) — also called a carrier if the recessive allele causes a disorder

Approach:

  1. Write out each parent's genotype (two alleles each)
  2. Put one parent's alleles across the top and the other's down the side
  3. Fill in the four boxes by combining the row and column alleles
  4. Count the genotypes and phenotypes to give ratios or percentages

Common pitfalls:

  • Forgetting that Bb and bB are the same genotype — count them together
  • Confusing genotype (letters) with phenotype (physical characteristic)
  • Not reading whether the question asks for a ratio, fraction, or percentage
  • In sex-linked inheritance, the allele is carried on the X chromosome — males have only one copy
steps: Write each parent's genotype (two alleles per parent)
Draw a 2×2 Punnett square grid with one parent's alleles across the top and the other down the side
Fill in the four boxes by combining row + column alleles
Count genotypes/phenotypes and express as a ratio, fraction, or percentage
Check: do the numbers add up to 4 offspring (or 100%)?

exam_context.frequency: Very common — Punnett squares appear on nearly every Paper 2

worked_examples.question: Two heterozygous parents (Bb × Bb) are crossed. Brown fur (B) is dominant to white fur (b). What percentage of offspring would you expect to have white fur?

steps.label: Step 2 — Count phenotypes
steps.content:
BB = brown, Bb = brown (dominant), Bb = brown, bb = white

3 brown : 1 white

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: 25% would have white fur (1 out of 4)

worked_examples.question: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). Two carrier parents (Ff × Ff) have a child. What is the probability that the child will have cystic fibrosis?

steps.label: Step 2 — Identify affected offspring
steps.content: Only ff has cystic fibrosis (homozygous recessive). That's 1 out of 4 boxes.

worked_examples.question: A couple has four children. Three have brown eyes and one has blue eyes. Blue eyes are recessive (bb). Determine the genotypes of both parents. Explain your reasoning.

steps.label: Step 1 — Work backwards from the offspring
steps.content: One child has blue eyes (bb). This means the child must have inherited one b from each parent.

steps.label: Step 2 — Determine parent genotypes
steps.content: Both parents must carry at least one b allele. Since both parents have brown eyes (dominant phenotype), they must each also carry one B allele.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Both parents are Bb (heterozygous). This gives a 3:1 ratio, matching 3 brown : 1 blue.

bronze.display: In a cross between two heterozygous parents (Bb × Bb), what ratio of offspring genotypes would you expect?

misconceptions.message: Bb × Bb gives: BB, Bb, Bb, bb — that's 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb.

bronze.display: Tall pea plants (T) are dominant to short (t). If two heterozygous plants (Tt × Tt) are crossed, what fraction of offspring would you expect to be short?

misconceptions.message: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Only tt is short = 1 out of 4 = 1/4.

bronze.display: What is the genotype of an organism that is homozygous dominant for a trait represented by the letter A?

misconceptions.message: Homozygous = two identical alleles. Dominant = capital letter. So homozygous dominant = AA.

bronze.display: A homozygous dominant parent (BB) is crossed with a homozygous recessive parent (bb). What percentage of offspring will be heterozygous (Bb)?

misconceptions.message: BB × bb: every box gives Bb. All 4 offspring are Bb = 100% heterozygous.

bronze.display: In a Bb × Bb cross, how many out of 4 offspring would you expect to show the dominant phenotype?

misconceptions.message: BB, Bb, Bb all show the dominant phenotype (the dominant allele is present). Only bb shows recessive. So 3 out of 4.

bronze.display: A parent with genotype Bb produces gametes. Which alleles can be in the gametes?

misconceptions.message: Each gamete gets one allele from each pair. A Bb parent produces gametes with either B or b, not both.

bronze.display: Two homozygous recessive parents (bb × bb) are crossed. What percentage of offspring will show the recessive phenotype?

misconceptions.message: bb × bb: every box gives bb. All offspring are homozygous recessive = 100%.

bronze.display: A Bb × Bb cross produces four offspring. What percentage of the offspring would you expect to be homozygous (either BB or bb)?

misconceptions.message: Both BB and bb are homozygous. From Bb × Bb: 1 BB + 2 Bb + 1 bb. Homozygous = BB + bb = 2 out of 4 = 50%.
Homozygous means two identical alleles — both BB and bb count. 1 BB + 1 bb = 2 out of 4 = 50%.

silver.display: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). Two parents who are both carriers (Ff) have a child. What is the percentage chance that the child is a carrier but does NOT have cystic fibrosis?

misconceptions.message: Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Carriers (Ff) = 2 out of 4 = 50%. Don't include ff (affected) or FF (not a carrier).

silver.display: In a cross Bb × bb, what percentage of offspring would you expect to show the recessive phenotype?

misconceptions.message: Bb × bb gives Bb, Bb, bb, bb. That's 2 dominant : 2 recessive = 50% recessive.

silver.display: Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele (D). A father with polydactyly (Dd) and an unaffected mother (dd) have children. What is the probability of a child having polydactyly?

misconceptions.message: Dd × dd gives Dd, Dd, dd, dd. Two have polydactyly (Dd) = 2 out of 4 = 50% = 1 in 2.

silver.display: If 200 offspring are produced from a Bb × Bb cross, how many would you expect to be homozygous recessive?

misconceptions.message: Bb × Bb gives 1/4 homozygous recessive (bb). 1/4 of 200 = 50 offspring.
The fraction that are bb is 1/4, not 1/2. 200 × 1/4 = 50.

silver.display: Tongue rolling (R) is dominant to non-rolling (r). A roller (Rr) and a non-roller (rr) have 80 children. How many would you expect to be non-rollers?

misconceptions.message: Rr × rr gives Rr, Rr, rr, rr. That's 2 out of 4 = 50% non-rollers. 50% of 80 = 40.

silver.display: Sickle cell trait is caused by allele Hb^S. A carrier (Hb^A Hb^S) and an unaffected person (Hb^A Hb^A) have children. What percentage could be carriers?

misconceptions.message: Hb^A Hb^S × Hb^A Hb^A gives: Hb^A Hb^A, Hb^A Hb^A, Hb^A Hb^S, Hb^A Hb^S. Two are carriers = 50%.

gold.display: A couple both have dimples (dominant trait, D). They have a child without dimples. What are the genotypes of both parents?

misconceptions.message: The child without dimples is dd, so inherited a d from each parent. Both parents show dimples (so have at least one D). Both must be Dd.
DD × DD can only produce DD children. DD × Dd cannot produce dd. Only Dd × Dd can give a dd child.

gold.display: Red flower colour (R) is incompletely dominant with white (W). Heterozygous (RW) produces pink flowers. If two pink flowers are crossed, what percentage of offspring will be pink?

misconceptions.message: RW × RW gives RR (red), RW (pink), RW (pink), WW (white). That's 2 pink out of 4 = 50%.
This is incomplete dominance — the heterozygote has a blend phenotype. RW × RW → 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.

gold.display: Colour blindness is sex-linked and recessive (carried on the X chromosome). A carrier mother (X^B X^b) and a normal father (X^B Y) have a son. What is the probability that the son is colour-blind?

misconceptions.message: Sons get their X from mum. Mum is X^B X^b, so 50% chance of passing X^b. A son with X^b Y is colour-blind. Probability = 50%.
The father's Y chromosome has no allele for this trait. The son's colour vision depends entirely on which X he gets from his mother.

gold.display: In a genetics experiment, 120 pea plants are produced from a monohybrid cross. 91 have round seeds and 29 have wrinkled seeds. What is the expected ratio, and does the actual data closely fit this ratio?
options: Expected 1:1 — no, the data does not fit
Expected 3:1 — no, 91:29 is too far from 90:30
Expected 1:3 — yes, the data fits well

misconceptions.message: 3:1 predicts 90 round : 30 wrinkled. Actual is 91:29. 91 ÷ 29 = 3.14:1, which is very close to 3:1.
Real data rarely matches predicted ratios exactly. 91:29 is close enough to 3:1 (predicted 90:30) to support the model.

gold.display: A man with blood type A (genotype I^A i) and a woman with blood type B (genotype I^B i) have children. What percentage of their children could have blood type O?

misconceptions.message: I^A i × I^B i gives: I^A I^B (AB), I^A i (A), I^B i (B), ii (O). One out of four = 25%.
I^A and I^B are codominant with each other, but both are dominant over i. Only ii gives type O blood.

gold.display: Two parents who are both heterozygous (Ff) for cystic fibrosis have 3 children, none of whom has the condition. What is the probability that their fourth child will have cystic fibrosis?

misconceptions.message: Each pregnancy is independent. Previous children don't affect the probability. Ff × Ff always gives a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of ff.
The previous 3 children being unaffected does NOT increase or decrease the chance for the fourth. It's still 25%.

title: Sampling, Mean and Percentage Change
description: Calculate means from data sets, work out percentage change, and estimate population size from quadrat data.

method_card.title: Sampling, Mean and Percentage Change
method_card.content:
These three calculations come up across both Biology papers — in ecology, experiments, and data analysis questions.

Mean: Add all the values together and divide by how many values there are. Always check for anomalous results (outliers) — the question may tell you to exclude them.

Percentage change: Shows how much a value has increased or decreased compared to the original. A negative answer means a decrease.

Population estimate: Used in ecology with quadrats. Find the mean count per quadrat, then scale up to the full area.

Common pitfalls:

  • Dividing by the wrong number when calculating the mean — count the number of data values carefully
  • Using the new value instead of the original as the denominator in percentage change
  • Forgetting to exclude anomalous results when told to
  • Mixing up the area of the quadrat with the total area in population estimates
steps: Read the question — are you finding a mean, percentage change, or population estimate?
For mean: add all values, then divide by how many there are (exclude anomalies if told to)
For population estimate: mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area)
Give your answer to the number of decimal places or significant figures asked for

exam_context.frequency: Very common — mean and percentage change appear on almost every paper; sampling in ecology questions

worked_examples.question: A student counts the number of daisies in 5 quadrats: 3, 7, 5, 4, 6. Calculate the mean number of daisies per quadrat.

steps.label: Step 2 — Divide by the number of values

worked_examples.question: A population of rabbits increases from 120 to 156 over one year. Calculate the percentage increase.
A student uses 0.5 m² quadrats in a field measuring 200 m². The number of buttercups in 10 quadrats was: 4, 6, 3, 5, 8, 5, 7, 4, 6, 2. Estimate the total population of buttercups in the field.

steps.label: Step 2 — Scale up to the full area
steps.content:
Number of quadrats that fit in the field = 200 ÷ 0.5 = 400

Population estimate = 5 × 400 = 2000

bronze.display: A student measures the height of 5 bean plants: 12 cm, 15 cm, 14 cm, 13 cm, 16 cm. Calculate the mean height.

misconceptions.message: Sum = 12 + 15 + 14 + 13 + 16 = 70. There are 5 values. Mean = 70 ÷ 5 = 14 cm.

bronze.display: A population of bacteria increases from 500 to 650. Calculate the percentage change.

misconceptions.message: Use the original value (500) as the denominator: (650 − 500) ÷ 500 × 100 = 150 ÷ 500 × 100 = 30%.
Don't forget to multiply by 100: 150 ÷ 500 = 0.3, then 0.3 × 100 = 30%.

bronze.display: Calculate the mean of these pulse rates (bpm): 68, 72, 74, 70, 66.

misconceptions.message: Sum = 68 + 72 + 74 + 70 + 66 = 350. There are 5 values. Mean = 350 ÷ 5 = 70 bpm.

bronze.display: The mass of a plant increases from 2.0 g to 2.8 g over 4 weeks. Calculate the percentage increase in mass.
Which of the following is an anomalous result in this data set: 12, 14, 13, 28, 15, 11?

misconceptions.message: Most values cluster around 11–15. The value 28 is far from the others — it's the anomaly.

bronze.display: A student counts daisies in 4 quadrats: 8, 5, 7, 4. Calculate the mean number of daisies per quadrat.

misconceptions.message: Sum = 8 + 5 + 7 + 4 = 24. There are 4 quadrats. Mean = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 per quadrat.

bronze.display: A woodland had 80 squirrels last year. This year there are 60. Calculate the percentage change.

misconceptions.message: The population decreased: (60 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = −20 ÷ 80 × 100 = −25%. The negative sign shows a decrease.
Always divide by the original value (80), not the new value (60). (60 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = −25%.

bronze.display: The number of dandelions counted in 6 quadrats was: 3, 5, 4, 6, 3, 3. Calculate the mean.

misconceptions.message: Sum = 3 + 5 + 4 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 24. There are 6 values. Mean = 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

silver.display: A student uses 0.25 m² quadrats in a field of 100 m². The mean number of clover plants per quadrat is 6. Estimate the total population of clover in the field.

misconceptions.message: Number of quadrats in field = 100 ÷ 0.25 = 400. Population = 6 × 400 = 2400.
Don't just multiply mean by total area. Divide total area by quadrat area first: 100 ÷ 0.25 = 400. Then 6 × 400 = 2400.

silver.display: A patient's blood glucose drops from 8.4 mmol/L to 5.6 mmol/L after insulin. Calculate the percentage decrease. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: Change = 5.6 − 8.4 = −2.8. Percentage = −2.8 ÷ 8.4 × 100 = −33.3%. The question asks for the decrease, so answer is 33.3%.
Divide by the original (8.4), not the new value (5.6). 2.8 ÷ 8.4 × 100 = 33.3%.

silver.display: Five students measured the length of an onion cell under a microscope: 0.12 mm, 0.14 mm, 0.11 mm, 0.38 mm, 0.13 mm. One result is anomalous. Calculate the mean excluding the anomalous result.

misconceptions.message: 0.38 mm is the anomaly — it's far from the others. Exclude it: (0.12 + 0.14 + 0.11 + 0.13) ÷ 4 = 0.50 ÷ 4 = 0.125 mm.
After excluding the anomaly, you have 4 values, not 5. Sum = 0.50, mean = 0.50 ÷ 4 = 0.125 mm.

silver.display: A student uses 1 m² quadrats in a meadow of 500 m². The number of plantain in 8 quadrats was: 3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 3, 5, 4. Estimate the total population in the meadow.

misconceptions.message: Quadrat area is 1 m², so total area ÷ quadrat area = 500 ÷ 1 = 500. Population = 4 × 500 = 2000.

silver.display: The heart rate of a runner increased from 72 bpm at rest to 162 bpm during exercise. Calculate the percentage increase.

misconceptions.message: A percentage increase can be over 100% — it just means the value more than doubled. 90 ÷ 72 × 100 = 125%.

silver.display: The enzyme amylase broke down 15 mg of starch in 5 minutes. At a higher temperature, it broke down 9 mg in the same time. Calculate the percentage decrease in starch breakdown.

misconceptions.message: Original = 15, new = 9. Change = 9 − 15 = −6. Percentage = −6 ÷ 15 × 100 = −40%. Decrease = 40%.
The question asks for percentage decrease, so give a positive number: 40%.

gold.display: In 2020 a lake had an estimated population of 450 fish. By 2023, the estimated population was 585. Between 2023 and 2025, it fell to 468. Calculate the percentage change from 2020 to 2025.

misconceptions.message: The question asks for the overall change from 2020 to 2025. Original = 450, final = 468. (468 − 450) ÷ 450 × 100 = 18 ÷ 450 × 100 = 4%.
Don't add the two separate percentage changes — just compare 2020 to 2025 directly: (468 − 450) ÷ 450 × 100 = 4%.

gold.display: A student uses 0.5 m² quadrats to sample a 300 m² field. In 10 quadrats they find: 2, 4, 3, 1, 5, 3, 4, 2, 3, 3 dandelions. The same field is surveyed a month later with results: 5, 7, 6, 4, 8, 6, 5, 7, 6, 6. Calculate the percentage change in estimated population.

misconceptions.message: You could also skip scaling: the population ratio is the same as the mean ratio. Mean went from 3 to 6 = 100% increase. But you must still use the correct % change formula.

gold.display: A farmer tests two fertilisers. Crop A yield increased from 3.2 tonnes to 4.8 tonnes. Crop B yield increased from 2.5 tonnes to 4.0 tonnes. Which fertiliser gave the greater percentage increase?

misconceptions.message: A had a bigger absolute increase (1.6 vs 1.5 tonnes), but B had a bigger percentage increase (60% vs 50%). Always compare percentages, not raw numbers.

gold.display: A student places 15 quadrats (each 0.25 m²) randomly in a 750 m² field. The total number of clover plants found across all 15 quadrats is 90. Estimate the population of clover in the field.

misconceptions.message: Mean per quadrat = 90 ÷ 15 = 6. Quadrats in field = 750 ÷ 0.25 = 3000. Population = 6 × 3000 = 18,000.
Total area ÷ quadrat area = 750 ÷ 0.25 = 3000 (not 750 ÷ 15). Mean = 6. Population = 6 × 3000 = 18,000.

gold.display: A scientist measures antibody concentration (arbitrary units) at 0, 7, 14, and 21 days after vaccination: 0.2, 1.4, 3.8, 3.6. Calculate the percentage change between day 0 and day 14.

misconceptions.message: The question asks for the change to day 14 (3.8), not day 21 (3.6). (3.8 − 0.2) ÷ 0.2 × 100 = 1800%.

gold.display: A student suggests that using more quadrats would make their population estimate more reliable. A second student says using larger quadrats would be better. Explain which student is more likely to improve reliability and why.
options: Student 1 — more quadrats gives a more representative sample of the whole area
Student 2 — larger quadrats cover more ground so the data is better
Both are equally valid — either approach works

misconceptions.message: More quadrats (more samples) gives a more representative mean, which improves reliability. Larger quadrats change what you measure but don't necessarily improve the reliability of the overall estimate.
Random placement reduces bias, but increasing the number of quadrats improves reliability by making the mean more representative.
